title: GitHub - aron98/load-lock: Machine-wide counting semaphore coordinating heavy work across parallel coding agents (OpenCode, Codex CLI, Claude Code, ...)
excerpt: Machine-wide counting semaphore coordinating heavy work across parallel coding agents (OpenCode, Codex CLI, Claude Code, ...) - aron98/load-lock
content_html:
A machine-wide heavy-work budget for parallel coding agents.

When several agents work side by side on one machine — separate sessions, repos, git worktrees, or harnesses (OpenCode, Codex CLI, Claude Code, ...) — their builds and test suites stomp on each other, thrash the caches, and starve each other's cores. load-lock gives them one shared counting semaphore: acquire a permit before heavy work, keep doing light work while queued, receive a FIFO offer when capacity frees, claim it, run, release. It is cooperative and advisory — no command wrapping, no automatic shell classification, no approval interruptions.

agent A (OpenCode)        agent B (Codex)         agent C (Claude Code)
  acquire "cargo test"      acquire "npm test"      acquire "build docs"
  granted ✓ runs            queued → keeps coding   queued → keeps coding
  ...                       offer → claim ✓ runs    (misses window → paused)
  release ✓                 release ✓               rejoin → offer → claim ✓

Three agents, one budget — the queue drains FIFO while everyone keeps coding:

Features

  • One budget for the whole machine — every client of any harness shares one capacity pool regardless of repo/worktree/cwd. Default: pool heavy, capacity 1; fully runtime-configurable by any agent via versioned CAS updates (persisted with author + rationale).
  • Atomic acquire-or-queue — single daemon event loop; a release can never slip between a failed check and queue registration.
  • FIFO offers with opaque claim tokens — outstanding offers reserve capacity; expired offers pass capacity to the next waiter and pause the absent request until it explicitly rejoins (no endless recycling).
  • Real process-lifecycle cleanup — permits attach to actual processes (pid + process group + /proc start time, PID-reuse-safe). Background jobs outliving the shell keep their permit until the whole group exits. Never auto-expired merely for being old. Untracked work uses an honest, documented heartbeat-lease tradeoff. Explicit release is always available and idempotent.
  • Crash-safe — agent crashes release tracked permits on confirmed process death; daemon restarts reconcile a journal against real liveness and auto-respawn transparently.
  • Honest notifications — tool-boundary offer delivery everywhere; real idle wakeup where the harness supports it (live-verified on OpenCode; hook-based on Claude Code and Codex CLI); a bounded blocking wait_for_turn (load-lock wait on the CLI) that sleeps until your turn and auto-claims for harnesses without idle wakeup; durable event ids for reconnects. A notification never authorizes work — only claim does.
  • Policy that actually reaches the model — installed per harness via its real mechanism (plugin context hook, SessionStart hooks incl. compact matchers, global instruction files), plus a detailed skill/guide.
  • Resource-aware — inspect_machine reports cgroup/container CPU and memory limits and current pressure; never assumes cores = capacity.

Quickstart

npm install -g @aron98/load-lock
load-lock install --harness opencode     # or claude-code | codex | gemini-cli |
                                         # copilot-cli | cline | roo-code | goose |
                                         # omac (sandbox grants) | generic
load-lock doctor

From then on, agents see the policy and tools automatically: OpenCode plugin (load_lock_* tools), Claude Code / Codex MCP tools (mcp__load-lock__*) plus session hooks. Any other MCP-capable harness can use the generic stdio server; plain shells use the CLI:

load-lock run --reason "nightly build" -- npm run build   # acquire→run→release
load-lock status                                          # machine-wide view
load-lock dashboard                                       # live read-only dashboard (q quits)
load-lock help                                            # one-screen usage of every command
load-lock configure --capacity 2 --reason "16-core host" --author me

OpenCode users also get a live dashboard inside the TUI: /load-lock opens it in-window, every session screen shows a clickable at-a-glance widget in the right sidebar, and the home screen has a footer indicator — same data, themed. See docs/OPERATIONS.md → "Dashboard".

Sandboxed agents

Agents running inside a sandbox (bubblewrap/omac, Docker, macOS seatbelt, WSL2) share the host's budget instead of getting their own: bridge the daemon's Unix socket into the sandbox, set LOAD_LOCK_NO_SPAWN=1 so the client never spawns a useless sandbox-local daemon, and optionally tag holds with LOAD_LOCK_LABEL_PREFIX (e.g. bwrap:issue-42 build). Ready-to-run per-sandbox recipes — live-verified for bubblewrap and omac, contract-inspected for the rest, plus the cross-PID-namespace lease lifecycle — live in docs/OPERATIONS.md → "Sandboxes".

Layout

src/core/       daemon + state machine + persistence + machine inspection
src/mcp/        MCP stdio server (universal adapter)
src/adapters/   OpenCode native plugin
src/cli/        CLI incl. installer, hook handlers, run/wait helpers
src/test/       32 tests: state machine, real multi-process daemon tests,
                MCP integration, hook contracts, run helper
demo/           reproducible 3-worktree demo (three agents, one pool)
docs/           ARCHITECTURE / COMPATIBILITY / OPERATIONS / AGENT_GUIDE
skills/         packaged skill

Documentation

  • docs/ARCHITECTURE.md — design, why a dedicated service (vs WorkOS Airlock / mic-lock / flock wrappers), atomicity, restart semantics, notification honesty, lifecycle tradeoffs.
  • docs/COMPATIBILITY.md — per-harness capability matrix with implemented / contract-tested / proposed labels.
  • docs/OPERATIONS.md — install, config, troubleshooting, recovery, daemon lifecycle, sandbox bridging.
  • docs/AGENT_GUIDE.md — the playbook for agents.
  • docs/ADAPTERS.md — how to write an adapter for a new harness, using the published library surface.

Status

  • Core daemon/protocol/CLI: implemented, 68 automated tests passing (multi-process daemons, real processes, restarts, races, expiry, PID-reuse, subprocess survival; plus 9 dashboard tests — view-model shaping, event-cursor resume across a daemon restart, reconnect, and a load-lock dashboard --once render smoke test).
  • OpenCode adapter: implemented and live-verified (tools, policy injection, compaction-proof context hook, execution-boundary wakeup with tokens, skill).
  • Claude Code adapter: implemented, contract-tested against documented hook JSON; not yet live-verified (harness not installed on the verification machine).
  • Codex CLI adapter: implemented and live-verified end-to-end in Docker (interactive TUI via pty: policy injection, MCP round-trip, FIFO queueing behind a competing holder, Stop-hook decision-block wakeup; see COMPATIBILITY.md for the two upstream/provider constraints the verification harness works around).
  • Tier-3 fallback installers (Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI, Cline, Roo Code, Goose): implemented merge-only installers (MCP stdio server entry into the harness's real config + a global instructions-file section/policy rule file), config-tested via temp-HOME round-trips; fallback tier (no hooks, no async push — no idle wakeup).
  • Cursor adapter: implemented (issue #6) — merge-only project-level installer (.cursor/mcp.json MCP entry, .cursor/hooks.json stop hook per the now- officially-documented hooks v1 contract, .cursor/rules/load-lock.mdc Always-apply rule) + hook cursor stop handler emitting {"followup_message":...} idle wakeup. Contract-tested, not live-verified (no Cursor on the verification machine).
  • Aider: researched; manual CLI tier. See COMPATIBILITY.md for the matrix.

Linux-first; macOS works with documented liveness-check limitations; Windows has a named-pipe transport adapter (implemented and unit-tested on Linux via platform injection; not yet verified on a Windows machine).

From then on, agents see the policy and tools automatically: OpenCode plugin (load_lock_* tools), Claude Code / Codex MCP tools (mcp__load-lock__*) plus session hooks. Any other MCP-capable harness can use the generic stdio server; plain shells use the CLI:

load-lock run --reason "nightly build" -- npm run build   # acquire→run→release
load-lock status                                          # machine-wide view
load-lock dashboard                                       # live read-only dashboard (q quits)
load-lock help                                            # one-screen usage of every command
load-lock configure --capacity 2 --reason "16-core host" --author me

OpenCode users also get a live dashboard inside the TUI: /load-lock opens it in-window, every session screen shows a clickable at-a-glance widget in the right sidebar, and the home screen has a footer indicator — same data, themed. See docs/OPERATIONS.md → "Dashboard".

Sandboxed agents

Agents running inside a sandbox (bubblewrap/omac, Docker, macOS seatbelt, WSL2) share the host's budget instead of getting their own: bridge the daemon's Unix socket into the sandbox, set LOAD_LOCK_NO_SPAWN=1 so the client never spawns a useless sandbox-local daemon, and optionally tag holds with LOAD_LOCK_LABEL_PREFIX (e.g. bwrap:issue-42 build). Ready-to-run per-sandbox recipes — live-verified for bubblewrap and omac, contract-inspected for the rest, plus the cross-PID-namespace lease lifecycle — live in docs/OPERATIONS.md → "Sandboxes".
